architectural_implications.after: Harness and model become a commodity, swappable layer behind an abstraction boundary; engineering investment shifts to enablement, telemetry, and workflow depth (skills/customization) with measurement designed to control for the individual.
architectural_implications.before: Platform teams treat model selection, benchmark ranking, and harness migration as a primary productivity program, with roadmap tied to adopting the newest frontier model.
architectural_implications.consequence: Procurement favors portability over lock-in, and platform roadmaps are justified by measured within-subject effects rather than by vendor benchmark deltas.
architectural_implications.observation: Model and harness account for <1% of output variance while individual and team factors dominate.

architectural_implications.after: Runtimes gain explicit token/step budgets per task, marginal-value accounting for extra turns, and escalation only where the saturating curve still has slope.
architectural_implications.before: Harness and agent runtimes optimize for more capability exercised — more context, more retries, more self-critique passes — and adoption is tracked as consumption growth.
architectural_implications.consequence: Cost control becomes a first-class harness responsibility, and 'more tokens' stops being proxy evidence of productivity.
architectural_implications.observation: Token spend yields sublinear output (10x tokens for 2x output).

architectural_implications.after: Evaluation infrastructure watches vendor default changes and capture them as natural experiments, using within-engineer pairing to isolate the component effect.
architectural_implications.before: Tooling evaluations rely on fleet-wide before/after averages and vendor benchmarks.
architectural_implications.consequence: Measurement pipeline (per-engineer normalization, cohort pairing) becomes part of the platform rather than an after-the-fact analytics exercise.
architectural_implications.observation: Default-model changes act as exogenous shocks with measurable, near-zero throughput effect.

article_ideas.angle: Reprice the AI platform roadmap using the variance split; show which line items survive and which are mis-scoped by construction.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders, platform/DevEx teams, and anyone signing AI tooling budgets
article_ideas.thesis: Platform roadmaps organized around adopting the newest frontier model are optimizing the smallest term in the decomposition: tool and harness together explain under 1% of output variance while the individual engineer explains 75% and the team environment 12%. Any AI productivity program that is not instrumented to control for the individual is measuring noise and will keep reporting deltas that are indistinguishable from cohort drift.
article_ideas.title: Your Model Upgrade Is a Rounding Error

article_ideas.angle: Reframe enablement as a measured intervention with an effect size, and specify how to instrument skill depth rather than license activation.
article_ideas.audience: Developer enablement, DevEx, and internal platform teams
article_ideas.thesis: The binding constraint on AI-assisted output is not access to capability but depth of use: only 12% of engineer-weeks reach high skill adoption, and those weeks run ~30% higher output. Closing an adoption gap on features that already exist is a larger and more attributable intervention than shipping new capability or waiting for the next model, so the metric that matters is feature-depth usage, not seat count.
article_ideas.title: The 12% Problem: Capability Ships Faster Than Adoption

article_ideas.angle: Economics of agentic loops: saturating returns, budget policy, and what a stop rule looks like in a runtime.
article_ideas.audience: Agent runtime and AI platform engineers, engineering finance partners
article_ideas.based_on: Token consumption has a saturating returns curve
article_ideas.thesis: Consumption growth is a cost metric that has been misfiled as a productivity metric. With the top decile spending ~10x the median tokens for ~2x the output, the correct engineering response is per-task token and step budgets plus marginal-value gating of extra agent turns — optimize output per token, not tokens per task, and stop treating rising usage as evidence of rising productivity.
article_ideas.title: Tokens Are Not a Productivity KPI

article_ideas.angle: Evaluation infrastructure as a standing natural-experiment detector rather than a post-hoc analytics exercise.
article_ideas.audience: Measurement/analytics engineers and engineering productivity researchers
article_ideas.thesis: When a vendor silently re-defaults the model behind your harness, you get an exogenous shock that removes self-selection — the cleanest instrument available for isolating a component-level effect. Teams that instrument for these shifts get causal estimates on model changes for free, while teams that run fleet-wide before/after comparisons keep paying for migrations whose measured effect is negligible or negative.
article_ideas.title: Free Experiments: Harvesting Vendor Default Changes

connections.relationship: A <1% treatment share dictates that only within-subject or stratified designs have statistical power, which changes how any tool or model rollout should be evaluated.

connections.connects_to: agent runtime budgeting and cost-of-outcome economics
connections.relationship: Sublinear return implies per-task token/step budgets and marginal-value gating of extra agent turns rather than open-ended consumption.
The largest controllable behavioral lever is under-exercised, making adoption depth a measurable intervention target rather than a training nicety.

connections.concept: natural experiment from vendor default changes
connections.connects_to: causal inference in engineering productivity research
connections.relationship: Exogenous platform defaults supply instrumented comparisons without self-selection, complementing correlational DORA/SPACE-style telemetry.
Because per-person variance dominates, tooling-normalized comparisons across engineers require individual baselines rather than fleet averages.

evidence_quotes.text: The tool (harness and model) accounts for less than 1% of output variance.
You (the individual engineer's characteristics) account for 75% of variance.
Where you work (company and team environment) accounts for 12% of variance.

core_insights.generalization: In any domain where a general-purpose capability (a model, a database, a cloud) is rapidly commoditized, the residual variance concentrates in the operator and the surrounding organization, not in the component. Vendor selection stops being a differentiator; enablement, telemetry, and environment become the levers.
core_insights.insight: Productivity output variance decomposes sharply: the tool (harness + model) explains <1%, skill/customization 3%, usage volume (token spend, active days) 9%, company/team environment 12%, and the individual engineer 75%. The hierarchy inverts the common assumption that model/harness selection is the primary lever.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It gives a quantitative prior for where to spend effort and budget: interventions aimed at model choice have a ceiling of ~1% of explainable variance, while per-engineer and per-team factors dominate by two orders of magnitude. Any roadmap or platform investment that assumes the opposite is mispriced.

evidence_quotes.text: The tool (harness and model) accounts for less than 1% of output variance.
You (the individual engineer's characteristics) account for 75% of variance.
Individual engineers differ even more, with a 3.5x spread between top and bottom percentiles.

core_insights.generalization: When the treatment effect is <1% of variance, only paired/within-subject designs (same engineer, alternating tool, or switchback tests) have power. This applies to evaluating any low-effect developer-productivity intervention: linters, IDEs, CI changes, coding agents.
core_insights.insight: Measurement-design consequence of the variance split: with 75% of variance attributable to the individual and <1% to the tool, naive between-subject tool comparisons are noise-dominated. Detecting a tool effect requires within-subject or individual-stratified designs, not aggregate before/after averages over a population of engineers.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Most internal 'does this tool/model help?' evaluations are run as fleet-wide before/after comparisons. Given this decomposition, such an experiment is guaranteed to be dominated by who happens to be in the window rather than what was deployed — producing nulls that get misread as 'the tool doesn't work' or false positives from cohort drift.

evidence_quotes.text: Cursor changing its default AI models and Grok usage spiking while overall output remained centered on zero.
Switching between model families (Opus, Sonnet, GPT/Codex) shows negligible or negative impact on PR throughput.

core_insights.generalization: Platform vendors changing defaults create free natural experiments. Instrumenting for these exogenous shifts is a cheap way to estimate component-level causal effects without running your own controlled trial — and to avoid paying for migrations that don't move outcomes.
core_insights.insight: Cursor's change of its default model produced a natural experiment: usage shifted massively toward Grok, yet merged-PR output remained centered on zero with no statistical correlation. Model-family switches (Opus/Sonnet/GPT-Codex) showed negligible or even negative throughput impact.
core_insights.why_it_matters: A forced, involuntary default change is the cleanest real-world instrument available for isolating model effect — it removes self-selection by the engineer. The null result under that instrument is stronger evidence than correlational benchmark-to-productivity claims, and it suggests model migrations are not a productivity project.

evidence_quotes.text: Token spend hits diminishing returns following a saturating curve resembling a rocket equation; top 10% users spend 10x more tokens to get 2x more output than the median.
How much you use it (token spend and active days) accounts for 9% of variance.

core_insights.generalization: For any loop where the model does more work per unit output (agentic retries, self-critique passes, extended context), expect a saturating curve. Harness design should optimize output per token rather than tokens per task; capacity planning should assume sublinear return.
core_insights.insight: Token consumption has a saturating returns curve: the top 10% of users spend ~10x more tokens to obtain ~2x more output relative to the median. Consumption is a real but sublinear input, not a proportional production function.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Directly bounds the economics of agentic and high-context workflows: adding more agent turns, more context, or more retries buys diminishing output at linear cost. It implies a concrete stop policy — budget tokens against expected marginal PRs, not against a 'more usage is better' adoption KPI.

evidence_quotes.text: only 12% of engineer weeks show high skill adoption, but high skill use correlates with a 30% output bump
How well you use it (skill use, customization, tricks) accounts for 3% of variance.

core_insights.generalization: For capability-rich tools, adoption distribution is bimodal and the head is small. The highest-ROI work is often closing the adoption gap for existing features rather than shipping new capability — measure feature-depth usage, not seat count.
core_insights.insight: Heavy skilled usage of the tool is rare — only 12% of engineer-weeks — but those weeks show ~30% higher output, creating a large gap between what is available and what is actually exercised. The bottleneck is adoption of advanced capability, not access to it.
core_insights.why_it_matters: The correlation magnitude (30%) and rarity (12%) indicate a sizeable, under-exploited lever that lives in user behavior and harness features (skills, customization, agentic features) rather than in model capability. It reframes enablement as a measurable, attributable intervention with a larger effect size than model upgrades.

evidence_quotes.text: Companies and engineering teams differ by about 2x in output at the same AI usage level.
Individual engineers differ even more, with a 3.5x spread between top and bottom percentiles.

core_insights.generalization: Layered variance: person > team > org-wide tooling. Interventions should be evaluated against the layer they act on; a tool that claims org-wide impact but lives at the <1% layer is mis-scoped by construction.
core_insights.insight: Environment effects are real but bounded: companies and teams differ by ~2x in output at the same AI usage level, while individual engineers span ~3.5x between top and bottom percentiles. The org-level spread is smaller than the person-level spread.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Quantifies the payoff of org/platform work versus individual work: team environment is worth roughly a 2x factor, so 'where you work' is a legitimate lever but cannot close the gap that individual capability creates. It also warns that team-level process changes should be expected to move output by tens of percent, not multiples.

evidence_quotes.text: The tool (harness and model) accounts for less than 1% of output variance.
You (the individual engineer's characteristics) account for 75% of variance.
Individual engineers differ even more, with a 3.5x spread between top and bottom percentiles.

deep_dives.research_question: Which designs (per-engineer switchback, alternating-week assignment, matched-pair cohorts) achieve adequate statistical power to detect a tool/model effect that is <1% of output variance, and what engineer count and time horizon does that require?
deep_dives.topic: Within-subject experiment design for sub-1% developer-tool effects
deep_dives.trigger_insight: naive between-subject tool comparisons are noise-dominated
deep_dives.why: Nearly all internal 'does this tool help?' evaluations are fleet-wide before/after averages. With 75% of variance sitting in the individual engineer, such tests are dominated by who happens to be in the window, producing nulls misread as 'the tool doesn't work' or cohort-drift false positives. A power analysis converts the variance split into an actual experimental protocol.

evidence_quotes.text: only 12% of engineer weeks show high skill adoption, but high skill use correlates with a 30% output bump
How well you use it (skill use, customization, tricks) accounts for 3% of variance.

deep_dives.research_question: Which specific skill invocations, custom instructions, and agentic patterns produce the reported 30% output bump, how much survives controlling for engineer identity, and what fraction retains effect after a model or harness switch?
deep_dives.topic: Decomposing the 30% high-skill bump: what counts as skill, and does it transfer?
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Heavy skilled usage of the tool is rare
deep_dives.why: The skill lever is the largest controllable non-human factor and is exercised in only 12% of engineer-weeks. But if the 30% is confounded with engineer ability, or if the customizations are brittle across model versions, enablement programs are being built on a correlation that will not replicate.

evidence_quotes.text: Token spend hits diminishing returns following a saturating curve resembling a rocket equation; top 10% users spend 10x more tokens to get 2x more output than the median.
How much you use it (token spend and active days) accounts for 9% of variance.

deep_dives.research_question: At what token/step budget does the marginal merged-PR-per-token curve fall below cost for agentic workflows, and does the saturation point shift when tasks are long-horizon and autonomous rather than interactive?
deep_dives.topic: Marginal value of tokens: where the saturation curve crosses the cost line
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Token consumption has a saturating returns curve
deep_dives.why: A 10x-spend-for-2x-output curve turns consumption growth into a cost KPI masquerading as a productivity KPI. Harness runtimes need explicit per-task budgets and marginal-value gating of extra turns, and capacity planning must assume sublinear return rather than proportional production.

evidence_quotes.text: Cursor changing its default AI models and Grok usage spiking while overall output remained centered on zero.
Switching between model families (Opus, Sonnet, GPT/Codex) shows negligible or negative impact on PR throughput.

deep_dives.research_question: How should evaluation infrastructure detect exogenous platform shocks (a vendor re-defaulting its model, a harness changing its agent loop) and pair engineers across the change to estimate component-level effects without self-selection?
deep_dives.topic: Vendor default changes as free causal instruments
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Cursor's change of its default model produced a natural experiment
deep_dives.why: A forced, involuntary default change removes self-selection and is the cleanest real-world instrument available for isolating a model effect. Systematically harvesting these shocks gives component-level causal estimates at near-zero cost, and prevents paying for migrations that do not move outcomes.

evidence_quotes.text: The tool (harness and model) accounts for less than 1% of output variance.
Companies and engineering teams differ by about 2x in output at the same AI usage level.

deep_dives.research_question: Does the <1% tool share and the 3%/9%/12%/75% split hold when the outcome is quality-weighted (revert rate, review iterations, incident attribution, review latency) rather than merged-PR count?
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Does merged-PR throughput capture quality, rework, or review burden
deep_dives.why: The entire result set rests on throughput as the sole outcome. A null on PR counts is not a null on engineering value: model or skill changes could shift output mix, rework, or reviewer burden while volume stays flat. Re-running the decomposition on quality-weighted outcomes is the cheapest test of whether the headline claim is metric-insensitivity in disguise.

project_ideas.name: Token Budget Governor
project_ideas.poc: Instrument a coding-agent runtime with per-task token/step budgets and a marginal-value gate that escalates past the budget only when historical output-per-token for that task class is still on the sloped part of the curve. A/B budgeted vs unbudgeted runs on a matched task set.

project_ideas.based_on: but those weeks show ~30% higher output
project_ideas.hypothesis: A small subset of specific skill invocations (custom instructions, particular agentic patterns) carries most of the 30% high-skill output bump, and that subset retains its effect after a model or harness swap, while most bespoke 'tricks' decay to zero.
project_ideas.measurement: Per-skill marginal output delta with CIs, share of the 30% bump attributable to the top-k skills, retention ratio of each skill's coefficient across the model switch, and adoption depth (12% baseline vs. post-enablement).

project_ideas.poc: Instrument individual skill and customization invocations per engineer-week, then estimate per-skill marginal output with engineer fixed effects; re-estimate the same coefficients across an observed model/harness change to measure retention.

project_ideas.based_on: Cursor's change of its default model produced a natural experiment

project_ideas.measurement: Effect size and CI per detected shift, time-to-detection after the vendor change, replication rate of the null, and migration coordination cost avoided per shift.
project_ideas.name: Default-Shift Watcher
project_ideas.poc: Build a watcher that detects harness/model default changes from release notes and telemetry fingerprints, auto-slices pre/post windows, and runs a paired within-engineer estimate with the migration window excluded from the learning-curve tail.

source.title: Better AI Models Won't Fix Your Engineering Team — Nicholas Arcolano, Jellyfish

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Nicholas Arcolano, Ph.D.
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Determinants of AI engineering productivity and output in software development
  • Purpose: To debunk the misconception that better AI models inherently improve software engineering output and to quantify the actual factors influencing engineering productivity when using AI coding assistants. Nicholas Arcolano, Head of AI and Research at Jellyfish, presents empirical research analyzing data from thousands of engineers and companies using AI coding tools. He addresses the widespread belief that upgrading AI models is the key productivity driver, demonstrating through statistical analysis that model choice and tool selection matter far less than engineer skill, token consumption volume, and organizational environment.

Topic Map

The Golf Analogy: Equipment vs. Fundamentals (38)

  • Explanation: Introduces a golf analogy to illustrate how engineers often blame their tools (seeking better clubs or models) when the fundamental problem is their own usage and fundamentals.
  • Key claims:
    • Golfers often think buying better clubs will fix their game.
    • Instructors emphasize that the player and fundamentals matter more than equipment.
    • Data shows PGA tour driving distances increased over time due to technology improvements like solid-core balls, but human skill remains paramount.
  • Examples:
    • PGA tour average driving distance increasing from 257 yards in 1980 to 306 yards in 2026.
  • Terminology:
    • solid-core ball era
    • PGA tour
  • Why it matters: Establishes the core thesis that focusing exclusively on upgrading AI models is often a distraction from improving how developers actually use tools.

The Model Frontier and the Cursor Natural Experiment (207)

  • Explanation: Examines how AI language models keep getting better over time, but contrasts this with empirical data from Jellyfish tracking the impact of a major model default change in Cursor.
  • Key claims:
    • Frontier language models are steadily improving in capability over time.
    • When SpaceX and other developers experienced a massive default shift toward Grok in Cursor, output metrics showed no statistical correlation or change.
    • Model changes alone do not automatically shift team-wide PR throughput.
  • Examples:
    • Artificial Analysis chart showing frontier language model intelligence growth.
    • Cursor changing its default AI models and Grok usage spiking while overall output remained centered on zero.
  • Terminology:
    • frontier language model
    • artificial analysis
    • merged PRs
    • natural experiment
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates that simply swapping underlying AI models yields negligible change in engineering output compared to other factors.

Deconstructing the Productivity Pie: What Actually Matters (453)

  • Explanation: Breaks down the statistical analysis of 50,000 engineers across 447 companies using Cursor, Claude Code, and other tools, quantifying the relative impact of five key factors on PR throughput.
  • Key claims:
    • The tool (harness and model) accounts for less than 1% of output variance.
    • How well you use it (skill use, customization, tricks) accounts for 3% of variance.
    • How much you use it (token spend and active days) accounts for 9% of variance.
    • Where you work (company and team environment) accounts for 12% of variance.
    • You (the individual engineer's characteristics) account for 75% of variance.
  • Examples:
    • Bar chart showing the percentage breakdown: The tool (<1%), How well you use it (3%), How much you use it (9%), Where you work (12%), You (75%).
  • Terminology:
    • PR throughput
    • token spend
    • active days
    • statistical correlation
  • Why it matters: Provides a data-driven hierarchy of factors influencing AI-assisted software engineering productivity.

Analyzing Specific Factors: Tool, Skill, Consumption, and Environment (720)

  • Explanation: Examines each factor from the productivity pie in detail, looking at model switches, skill adoption rates, token consumption diminishing returns, and organizational variance.
  • Key claims:
    • Switching between model families (Opus, Sonnet, GPT/Codex) shows negligible or negative impact on PR throughput.
    • Heavy skill use is still rare; only 12% of engineer weeks show high skill adoption, but high skill use correlates with a 30% output bump.
    • Token spend hits diminishing returns following a saturating curve resembling a rocket equation; top 10% users spend 10x more tokens to get 2x more output than the median.
    • Companies and engineering teams differ by about 2x in output at the same AI usage level.
    • Individual engineers differ even more, with a 3.5x spread between top and bottom percentiles.
  • Examples:
    • Chart comparing Opus, Sonnet, and GPT/Codex switch outcomes.
    • Token spend diminishing returns scatter plot showing median vs top 10%.
    • Distribution histograms for company and individual engineer productivity relative to typical.
  • Terminology:
    • skill use
    • token spend
    • diminishing returns
    • saturating curve
    • PR throughput
    • quartile
  • Why it matters: Explains the nuances behind why individual developer habits and team environment dominate AI productivity outcomes.

Key Points

Model choice accounts for less than 1% of productivity variance

  • Explanation: Empirical data from thousands of developers shows that switching between top-tier models (Opus, Sonnet, GPT, Grok) has virtually no statistically significant impact on weekly merged PR throughput.
  • Evidence: Jellyfish research dataset across 49k engineers at 447 companies.
  • Practical implication: Engineering leaders should stop obsessing over benchmark scores of new models when evaluating developer productivity.

Skill use and proficiency amplify output significantly

  • Explanation: While heavy skill adoption is rare (only 12% of engineer weeks), engineers who master advanced tool usage see up to a 30% increase in merged PRs.
  • Evidence: Analysis of skill run frequency per week versus PR throughput.
  • Practical implication: Invest in training developers how to effectively use AI coding harnesses and agentic features rather than just providing access to models.

Token consumption hits diminishing returns

  • Explanation: Spending more tokens correlates with higher output up to a point, but follows a saturating curve where a 10x increase in token spend yields only a 2x increase in output for top users vs. the median.
  • Evidence: Data from AI Engineer World's Fair talk showing token spend vs. merged PRs per day.
  • Practical implication: Blindly increasing API consumption or prompt volume yields diminishing financial and productivity returns.

Individual engineers and teams matter more than technology

  • Explanation: 75% of output variance is driven by the individual engineer, and 12% by the company environment, dwarfing the impact of the tool itself.
  • Evidence: Statistical decomposition of variance across 50k engineers.
  • Practical implication: Focus on engineering culture, individual workflows, and team processes rather than expecting AI tools to automatically elevate low-performing teams.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The AI Engineering Productivity Attribution Model

  • How it works: A variance decomposition framework measuring what drives changes in merged PRs per engineer per week based on tool, skill adoption, token volume, company, and individual factors.
  • Components:
    • The tool (<1%)
    • How well you use it (3%)
    • How much you use it (9%)
    • Where you work (12%)
    • You (75%)
  • When to use: When evaluating investments in AI coding assistants and diagnosing why developer productivity is or is not improving.

Examples & Case Studies

SpaceX and other companies transitioned to Grok as defaults changed in Cursor.

## Overview
- **Speaker**: Nicholas Arcolano, Ph.D.
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: Determinants of AI engineering productivity and output in software development
- **Purpose**: To debunk the misconception that better AI models inherently improve software engineering output and to quantify the actual factors influencing engineering productivity when using AI coding assistants.
Nicholas Arcolano, Head of AI and Research at Jellyfish, presents empirical research analyzing data from thousands of engineers and companies using AI coding tools. He addresses the widespread belief that upgrading AI models is the key productivity driver, demonstrating through statistical analysis that model choice and tool selection matter far less than engineer skill, token consumption volume, and organizational environment.
## Topic Map
### The Golf Analogy: Equipment vs. Fundamentals (38)
- **Explanation**: Introduces a golf analogy to illustrate how engineers often blame their tools (seeking better clubs or models) when the fundamental problem is their own usage and fundamentals.
- **Key claims**:
  - Golfers often think buying better clubs will fix their game.
  - Instructors emphasize that the player and fundamentals matter more than equipment.
  - Data shows PGA tour driving distances increased over time due to technology improvements like solid-core balls, but human skill remains paramount.
- **Examples**:
  - PGA tour average driving distance increasing from 257 yards in 1980 to 306 yards in 2026.
- **Terminology**:
  - solid-core ball era
  - PGA tour
- **Why it matters**: Establishes the core thesis that focusing exclusively on upgrading AI models is often a distraction from improving how developers actually use tools.
### The Model Frontier and the Cursor Natural Experiment (207)
- **Explanation**: Examines how AI language models keep getting better over time, but contrasts this with empirical data from Jellyfish tracking the impact of a major model default change in Cursor.
- **Key claims**:
  - Frontier language models are steadily improving in capability over time.
  - When SpaceX and other developers experienced a massive default shift toward Grok in Cursor, output metrics showed no statistical correlation or change.
  - Model changes alone do not automatically shift team-wide PR throughput.
- **Examples**:
  - Artificial Analysis chart showing frontier language model intelligence growth.
  - Cursor changing its default AI models and Grok usage spiking while overall output remained centered on zero.
- **Terminology**:
  - frontier language model
  - artificial analysis
  - merged PRs
  - natural experiment
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates that simply swapping underlying AI models yields negligible change in engineering output compared to other factors.
### Deconstructing the Productivity Pie: What Actually Matters (453)
- **Explanation**: Breaks down the statistical analysis of 50,000 engineers across 447 companies using Cursor, Claude Code, and other tools, quantifying the relative impact of five key factors on PR throughput.
- **Key claims**:
  - The tool (harness and model) accounts for less than 1% of output variance.
  - How well you use it (skill use, customization, tricks) accounts for 3% of variance.
  - How much you use it (token spend and active days) accounts for 9% of variance.
  - Where you work (company and team environment) accounts for 12% of variance.
  - You (the individual engineer's characteristics) account for 75% of variance.
- **Examples**:
  - Bar chart showing the percentage breakdown: The tool (<1%), How well you use it (3%), How much you use it (9%), Where you work (12%), You (75%).
- **Terminology**:
  - PR throughput
  - token spend
  - active days
  - statistical correlation
- **Why it matters**: Provides a data-driven hierarchy of factors influencing AI-assisted software engineering productivity.
### Analyzing Specific Factors: Tool, Skill, Consumption, and Environment (720)
- **Explanation**: Examines each factor from the productivity pie in detail, looking at model switches, skill adoption rates, token consumption diminishing returns, and organizational variance.
- **Key claims**:
  - Switching between model families (Opus, Sonnet, GPT/Codex) shows negligible or negative impact on PR throughput.
  - Heavy skill use is still rare; only 12% of engineer weeks show high skill adoption, but high skill use correlates with a 30% output bump.
  - Token spend hits diminishing returns following a saturating curve resembling a rocket equation; top 10% users spend 10x more tokens to get 2x more output than the median.
  - Companies and engineering teams differ by about 2x in output at the same AI usage level.
  - Individual engineers differ even more, with a 3.5x spread between top and bottom percentiles.
- **Examples**:
  - Chart comparing Opus, Sonnet, and GPT/Codex switch outcomes.
  - Token spend diminishing returns scatter plot showing median vs top 10%.
  - Distribution histograms for company and individual engineer productivity relative to typical.
- **Terminology**:
  - skill use
  - token spend
  - diminishing returns
  - saturating curve
  - PR throughput
  - quartile
- **Why it matters**: Explains the nuances behind why individual developer habits and team environment dominate AI productivity outcomes.
## Key Points
### Model choice accounts for less than 1% of productivity variance
- **Explanation**: Empirical data from thousands of developers shows that switching between top-tier models (Opus, Sonnet, GPT, Grok) has virtually no statistically significant impact on weekly merged PR throughput.
- **Evidence**: Jellyfish research dataset across 49k engineers at 447 companies.
- **Practical implication**: Engineering leaders should stop obsessing over benchmark scores of new models when evaluating developer productivity.
### Skill use and proficiency amplify output significantly
- **Explanation**: While heavy skill adoption is rare (only 12% of engineer weeks), engineers who master advanced tool usage see up to a 30% increase in merged PRs.
- **Evidence**: Analysis of skill run frequency per week versus PR throughput.
- **Practical implication**: Invest in training developers how to effectively use AI coding harnesses and agentic features rather than just providing access to models.
### Token consumption hits diminishing returns
- **Explanation**: Spending more tokens correlates with higher output up to a point, but follows a saturating curve where a 10x increase in token spend yields only a 2x increase in output for top users vs. the median.
- **Evidence**: Data from AI Engineer World's Fair talk showing token spend vs. merged PRs per day.
- **Practical implication**: Blindly increasing API consumption or prompt volume yields diminishing financial and productivity returns.
### Individual engineers and teams matter more than technology
- **Explanation**: 75% of output variance is driven by the individual engineer, and 12% by the company environment, dwarfing the impact of the tool itself.
- **Evidence**: Statistical decomposition of variance across 50k engineers.
- **Practical implication**: Focus on engineering culture, individual workflows, and team processes rather than expecting AI tools to automatically elevate low-performing teams.

### The AI Engineering Productivity Attribution Model
